solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(2.94 \times 10^{-10}\) C, which carries the right digits with an exponent smaller by \(10^{3}\). The decisive check is the stem's own force: putting a charge of \(1.47 \times 10^{-10}\) C on each sphere returns \(F \approx 6 \times 10^{-9}\) N, not the \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) N the question states. The total charge on the two spheres is \(2.94 \times 10^{-7}\) C.]

Both spheres carry equal negative charges, say \(-q\) each, so the magnitude of the repulsive force between them is
\(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q^{2}}{r^{2}}\)

Given \(F = 6 \times 10^{-3}\) N and \(r = 18\) cm \(= 0.18\) m,
\(q^{2} = \dfrac{Fr^{2}}{9 \times 10^{9}} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-3} \times (0.18)^{2}}{9 \times 10^{9}} = \dfrac{1.944 \times 10^{-4}}{9 \times 10^{9}} = 2.16 \times 10^{-14}\)
\(q = \sqrt{2.16 \times 10^{-14}} = 1.47 \times 10^{-7}\) C

The question asks for the TOTAL charge on both spheres, so
total charge \(= 2q = 2.94 \times 10^{-7}\) C
and since both charges are negative this is \(-2.94 \times 10^{-7}\) C.

The value printed in the book, \(2.94 \times 10^{-10}\) C, carries the same digits but an exponent smaller by \(10^{3}\). Substituting a charge of \(1.47 \times 10^{-10}\) C back into Coulomb's law returns a force of about \(6 \times 10^{-9}\) N, not the \(6 \times 10^{-3}\) N the question states.

[Textbook misprint: the stem says "a force of magnitude \(-0.2\) N". A magnitude is never negative; the minus sign is carrying the attractive sense of the force between the unlike charges \(+q\) and \(-2q\). It is read here as an attractive force of magnitude \(0.2\) N, which is what the printed key also assumes.]

The two charges have magnitudes \(q\) and \(2q\), so by Coulomb's law the magnitude of the force between them is
\(|F| = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q \times 2q}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9}\,q^{2}}{r^{2}}\)

Given \(|F| = 0.2\) N and \(r = 25.0\) cm \(= 0.25\) m,
\(q^{2} = \dfrac{|F|\,r^{2}}{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9}} = \dfrac{0.2 \times 0.0625}{1.8 \times 10^{10}} = \dfrac{1.25 \times 10^{-2}}{1.8 \times 10^{10}} = 6.944 \times 10^{-13}\)
\(q = \sqrt{6.944 \times 10^{-13}} = 8.333 \times 10^{-7}\) C

\(q = 8.333 \times 10^{-7}\) C \(= 0.8333\ \mu\)C

The charges are \(+q\) and \(-2q\), which are unlike, so the force between them is attractive. The stem's phrase "a force of magnitude \(-0.2\) N" should be read as an attractive force of magnitude 0.2 N: a magnitude is never negative, and the minus sign is carrying the attractive sense.

By symmetry every one of the four charges experiences a force of the same magnitude, directed outward along the diagonal through its own corner. Take any one corner, with \(q = 6 \times 10^{-8}\) C on each and side \(a = 3\) cm \(= 0.03\) m.

Force due to each of the two ADJACENT charges, at distance \(a\):
\(F_{1} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (6 \times 10^{-8})^{2}}{(0.03)^{2}} = \dfrac{3.24 \times 10^{-5}}{9 \times 10^{-4}} = 3.6 \times 10^{-2}\) N
These two forces are mutually perpendicular (they act along the two sides), so their resultant is
\(\sqrt{2}\,F_{1} = 1.414 \times 3.6 \times 10^{-2} = 5.09 \times 10^{-2}\) N, directed along the diagonal.

Force due to the charge at the OPPOSITE corner, at distance \(a\sqrt{2}\):
\(F_{2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (6 \times 10^{-8})^{2}}{(0.03\sqrt{2})^{2}} = \dfrac{3.24 \times 10^{-5}}{1.8 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\) N
This acts along the same diagonal and in the same outward sense, so the two add directly:
\(F = \sqrt{2}\,F_{1} + F_{2} = 5.09 \times 10^{-2} + 1.8 \times 10^{-2} = 6.89 \times 10^{-2}\) N

The resultant force on each charge is \(6.89 \times 10^{-2}\) N, directed outward along the diagonal through that corner, away from the centre of the square. On a diagram drawn to scale the four arrows point outward along the two diagonals, one from each corner.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives (a) \(5.0 \times 10^{-2}\) V m and (c) \(3.5 \times 10^{-2}\) V m, which are exactly what these expressions return for a field of \(5.0\) N/C rather than the \(5.0\) kN/C the stem prints; both are low by \(10^{3}\). Case (b) is zero on either reading. Two things point at the key rather than at the stem: Q.3 (i) of this same block is also low by \(10^{3}\), and this is the standard flux exercise (a \(10\) cm square in a uniform field of a few kN/C), where the kilo prefix is deliberate. The answer above follows the stem as printed. Note separately that the stem writes \(\vec{E} = 5.0\) kN/C, equating a vector to a scalar and stating no direction; the three cases only make sense if \(\vec{E}\) is along the Z axis.]

The flux through a plane surface placed in a uniform field is
\(\phi = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{S} = ES\cos\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the field and the NORMAL to the surface, not the surface itself.

\(E = 5.0\) kN/C \(= 5.0 \times 10^{3}\) N/C; side \(= 10.0\) cm \(= 0.100\) m, so \(S = (0.100)^{2} = 1.00 \times 10^{-2}\) m\(^{2}\).
The three cases only make sense if the field points along the Z axis, which is what case (c) presumes; the stem as printed gives \(\vec{E}\) a magnitude but no direction.

(a) The square lies in the XY plane, so its normal is along Z, parallel to the field, and \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\):
\(\phi = ES\cos 0^{\circ} = 5.0 \times 10^{3} \times 1.00 \times 10^{-2} = 50\) V m

(b) The square lies in the XZ plane, so its normal is along Y, perpendicular to the field, and \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\):
\(\phi = ES\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\)
The field lines graze the surface without crossing it, so the flux is zero.

(c) The normal makes \(45^{\circ}\) with the Z axis, so \(\theta = 45^{\circ}\):
\(\phi = ES\cos 45^{\circ} = 5.0 \times 10^{3} \times 1.00 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.7071 = 35.4\) V m

The values printed in the book for (a) and (c), \(5.0 \times 10^{-2}\) V m and \(3.5 \times 10^{-2}\) V m, are what these same expressions give for a field of \(5.0\) N/C rather than the \(5.0\) kN/C the stem states; they are smaller than the values above by a factor of \(10^{3}\). Case (b) is zero on either reading.

First locate the right angle. The sides 15 cm, 20 cm and 25 cm satisfy \(15^{2} + 20^{2} = 225 + 400 = 625 = 25^{2}\), so the triangle is right-angled with 25 cm as the hypotenuse and the right angle between the sides of 15 cm and 20 cm.

The charge at the \(90^{\circ}\) vertex is therefore 15 cm from one of the other charges and 20 cm from the other, and the two forces on it act along those two sides, which are mutually perpendicular.

With \(q = 10 \times 10^{-8}\) C \(= 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\) C on each charge,
\(F_{1} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-7})^{2}}{(0.15)^{2}} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{-5}}{2.25 \times 10^{-2}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\) N
\(F_{2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-7})^{2}}{(0.20)^{2}} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{-5}}{4.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 2.25 \times 10^{-3}\) N

Being perpendicular, they combine by Pythagoras:
\(F = \sqrt{F_{1}^{2} + F_{2}^{2}} = \sqrt{(4.0 \times 10^{-3})^{2} + (2.25 \times 10^{-3})^{2}} = \sqrt{2.106 \times 10^{-5}} = 4.59 \times 10^{-3}\) N

The force exerted on the charge at the right angle is \(4.59 \times 10^{-3}\) N. All three charges have the same sign, so it is repulsive, directed away from the other two; it makes an angle \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.25}{4.0}\right) = 29.4^{\circ}\) with the direction of \(F_{1}\).

(a) The plates are parallel, so the field between them is uniform and is given by
\(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\)
Given \(V = 5000\) V and \(d = 5\) cm \(= 5 \times 10^{-2}\) m,
\(E = \dfrac{5000}{5 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.0 \times 10^{5}\) V/m \(= 1.0 \times 10^{5}\) N/C

(b) The electric force on the oil drop is
\(F = qE = 9.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{5} = 9.6 \times 10^{-14}\) N

So the electric field intensity between the plates is \(1.0 \times 10^{5}\) N/C and the electric force on the oil drop is \(9.6 \times 10^{-14}\) N. This is the electric force alone; the drop also has its weight acting on it, which the question does not ask about.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(2.88 \times 10^{-2}\) N/C, the right digits with an exponent smaller by \(10^{7}\). \(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-8}}{(0.05)^{2}} = 2.88 \times 10^{5}\) N/C.]

The magnitude of the electric field due to a point charge at a distance \(r\) from it is
\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{|q|}{r^{2}}\)

Given \(|q| = 8.0 \times 10^{-8}\) C and \(r = 5.0\) cm \(= 5.0 \times 10^{-2}\) m,
\(E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-8}}{(5.0 \times 10^{-2})^{2}} = \dfrac{7.2 \times 10^{2}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 2.88 \times 10^{5}\) N/C

The magnitude of the electric field is \(2.88 \times 10^{5}\) N/C. Because the charge is negative, the field is directed radially INWARD, that is towards the charge, whereas the field of a positive charge points radially outward.

The value printed in the book, \(2.88 \times 10^{-2}\) N/C, has the same digits but an exponent smaller by \(10^{7}\).
